data: This section proves that repository-owned Forge documentation can use Hextra’s normal documentation layout without copying the source into this experiment.

Experiment source: brainboxemb/lib.py.solidcraft.forge@156a4bfd316dbe711932f58990328e5711385751, file docs/api.md.
The content below is rendered directly from that pinned Forge file.
Forge API Primary cross-object API contract. This document defines stable user-facing Forge/SCPF semantics that span more than one public Python object. Exact exported names, signatures, defaults and enum members come from the current Python implementation and its public docstrings. The generated API reference and agent index are derived from those implementation sources.
When implementation and this cross-object contract disagree, treat that as documentation/API drift to be resolved explicitly; do not silently preserve obsolete wording from this document.
SCPF exposes CAD objects and relationships, not JSON commands, transports, or an independent geometry engine. SolidCraft creates and evaluates the actual geometry.
data.at#at():
at() is geometric placement/alignment.
pin = Cylinder(d=8, h=20, axis=Axis.X).at(10, 0, 5) centered = Cylinder(d=8, h=30, axis=Axis.X).at(body) shape.at(target) means CENTER-to-CENTER for supported direct shapes. It does not mean “put this on a face”. Use on() or Sketch(on=...) for that intent.
data.attach#attach():
attach() is reserved for explicit relationships between reusable component occurrences in an assembly. It is the public Forge relationship; SolidCraft joint.create is an internal lowering detail.
right = Block().attach( left, parent=Anchor.RIGHT, child=Anchor.LEFT, ) A local planar offset=(u, v) on an attachment is measured in the attachment frame, not in world XY.
Forge generates replayable SolidCraft 0.42 commands and never makes up occurrence names such as Block:2. Every physical occurrence has a stable Forge-side id and a deterministic replay variable. During live execution or later replay, component.create and occurrence.copy bind those variables to the actual SolidCraft occurrence ids before a joint command uses them.
Copied occurrences can therefore be valid attachment endpoints without predicting browser numbering. The replay document still contains only the variable name; concrete runtime ids remain in the separate replay log.
A normal attachment currently requires both parent and child Placement rotations to be None. Forge does not yet transform every Anchor, AnchorFrame and AnchorTopology point/axis through occurrence rotation, so a rotated parent or child is rejected before command lowering rather than using a translation-only approximation. Ordinary rotated Placement remains supported outside normal attachments. as_built=True also remains compatible with rotated Placement because it relates already-positioned occurrences and does not lower anchor frames.
Chained normal attachments remain unsupported until their SolidCraft solve and replay order has been qualified. See change 0010, change 0013 and change 0017.
data.direction-face-and-anchor-vocabulary#Dir:
Cardinal direction names are shared where their geometric meaning is shared: TOP, BOTTOM, LEFT, RIGHT, FRONT, BACK.
Faces selects a surface for within-component feature placement. Anchor describes an attachment/alignment reference. Direction selectors may be composed, for example BOTTOM + LEFT. Component anchors may identify a face or a rectangular corner such as FRONT_TOP_RIGHT. AnchorFrame is an oriented local attachment coordinate frame: origin locates the datum, z gives its facing direction and x fixes clocking. AnchorFrame( origin=(10, 25, 0), z=RIGHT, x=UP, ) Put an anchor on a reusable component only when the datum is intrinsic to that physical component. If the datum exists only because of one assembly, the assembly owns the AnchorFrame.
data.explicit-sketch#Explicit Sketch:
An explicit Sketch is user-authored 2D design intent. It is not an implementation detail of a 3D primitive.
with Sketch(name="Rounded pad", on=body, parent=Anchor.TOP) as pad: pad.add( RoundedRectangle2D(40, 30, 5), anchor=CENTER, ) body = body + pad.extrude(8) For Sketch(on=target, parent=Anchor.TOP):
Forge asks SolidCraft for the current body faces and selects the unique largest planar +Z face; Forge passes SolidCraft’s returned face pick and face index to native sketch.create; SolidCraft owns the persistent face attachment and the sketch’s local coordinate frame; Forge passes authored profile coordinates directly in that native sketch frame instead of adding a reconstructed face-centre offset; project_edges=False is explicit so the result does not depend on a session setting; anchor=None means use the profile type’s defined default; for Circle2D, Rectangle2D and RoundedRectangle2D that default is CENTER; explicit anchor=CENTER centres a dimension-defined profile on the sketch origin; a numeric offset=(u, v) is reserved for a real design displacement. Therefore code such as offset=(-width/2, -depth/2) used only to emulate centering is a smell. Circle2D, Rectangle2D and RoundedRectangle2D use CENTER when anchor is omitted; offset=(u, v) is applied afterwards as a real local design displacement.
Polygon2D is different because its vertex coordinates already define its sketch-local placement. Text2D likewise uses SolidCraft’s text insertion point. For these coordinate-defined profiles an omitted anchor remains None, so Forge does not invent a profile centre. Text2D may still use Sketch.add(..., offset=(u, v)) to set its native insertion-point displacement. Explicit anchor=CENTER is not supported for Polygon2D or Text2D yet. Polygon2D keeps its existing offset/lowering limits.
Semantic profile centering was introduced by change 0018. The profile-specific omitted-anchor rule that preserves coordinate-defined Text2D placement is recorded in change 0020.
Selective Sketch extrusion uses SolidCraft’s own profile selection. Pass fixed sketch-local points with Sketch.extrude(..., profiles=[(x, y), ...]). Forge sends those points as native solid.extrude profiles selections; it does not expose profile indices or generated curve ids. SolidCraft 0.42 stores successful point selections by their surrounding curves where possible, so the selected profile can be found again when the saved design recomputes. exact_regions=True requests the exact region containing each point.
Profile pick points are fixed numeric authoring picks, not editable Forge Parameters. SolidCraft 0.42’s point-selection command field accepts numeric Sketch coordinates rather than parameter expressions.
A direct 3D primitive such as Box remains a native primitive; Forge must not synthesize an unnecessary Sketch merely to construct it.
data.features-and-operations#Features and ope: + joins/adds the described CAD feature to the model; Hole intent lowers to a cut. - expresses subtraction/cut where supported. & expresses intersection where supported. shell(), fillet() and chamfer() are modifiers of supported feature trees. rectangular_pattern() and circular_pattern() repeat already-applied native history features. Both keep one native SolidCraft pattern feature instead of expanding independent Python copies. Circular patterns support principal or fixed XYZ axes plus an optional fixed axis origin; native construction/edge/face axis selectors are separate future extensions. fillet(..., edges=...) and chamfer(..., edges=...) use the same edge-selection vocabulary where SolidCraft accepts the same edge picks: Edges.VERTICAL, supported two-direction Box edge selectors, Edges.from_profile(...), Edges.from_vertices(...) and explicit XYZ edge picks. Lip, SnapFit, Boss and Rest are object-level feature intents; the compiler chooses the appropriate native SolidCraft representation. Anchor.INNER_BOTTOM refers to the inner floor of a shelled body. X.MIN/CENTER/MAX and Y.MIN/CENTER/MAX express placement relative to parent bounds rather than copied world coordinates.
data.group#group():
group(name) changes only the SolidCraft browser hierarchy.
Forge represents the group with an empty SolidCraft component and explicitly sets that group to grounded=false. Grouping must not add a joint, Placement or solver constraint.
If the physical root occurrence is inside a group, grouping itself does not change its grounding decision. The empty group does not become the fixed part. For SolidCraft 0.42, a root occurrence with parameter-driven Placement remains ungrounded so its occurrence move can follow later parameter changes.
One reusable definition may have occurrences in different groups. Forge uses SolidCraft 0.42 occurrence.copy(parent=...) when a later copy belongs under a different group or back at the design root. The component definition remains shared.
See change 0011.
data.modelling-style-object-first-assemblies-:
Forge is deliberately object-first at the component/assembly level and expression-first inside component geometry.
At assembly level, named Python objects represent meaningful physical occurrences:
left = Board() right = left.copy( placement=Placement(x=160) ) bracket = CornerBracket().attach(left, ...) The variables represent parts in the design, so later relationships refer to the actual Python occurrence object rather than a generated SolidCraft label.
Inside one component, geometry remains a lightweight feature/expression model:
class Board: def build(self): body = Box(self.width, self.depth, self.height) holes = Hole(d=5, depth=Depth.THROUGH_ALL).repeat_linear(...) return body - holes Do not turn every primitive or feature into an assembly object. Conversely, do not flatten physical assembly parts into an anonymous transform expression tree. This boundary is intentional and is part of the Forge API design.
data.native-history-patterns#Native history p:
rectangular_pattern() and circular_pattern() operate on already-applied native history features rather than expanding independent Python copies. Circular patterns support the currently documented principal/fixed XYZ axis and optional fixed axis origin forms.
See change 0036.
data.native-hole-family#Native Hole family:
Forge exposes explicit native hole intent rather than requiring a caller to construct every recess or thread from Boolean primitives:
Hole(*, d, depth=Depth.THROUGH_ALL, direction=None) CounterboreHole( *, d, counterbore_d, counterbore_depth, depth=Depth.THROUGH_ALL, direction=None, ) CountersinkHole( *, d, countersink_d, countersink_angle=90, depth=Depth.THROUGH_ALL, direction=None, ) ThreadedHole( *, thread, depth=Depth.THROUGH_ALL, d=None, direction=None, hand="right", thread_depth=None, modeled=False, ease_out=None, ) The simple Hole remains compatible with the existing face-relative repeated hole path. The explicit native Hole-family constructors are positioned with at() and keep their recess/thread intent in one native feature.
See change 0037.
data.native-primitive-anchor-datum#Native pri:
Direct standard 3D primitives use CENTER as their constructor datum:
box = Box(80, 50, 10) pin = Cylinder(d=8, h=20) ball = Sphere(12) The public signatures are:
Box(length, width, thickness, *, anchor=Anchor.CENTER) Cylinder(*, d, h, axis=Axis.Z, anchor=Anchor.CENTER) Cone(*, d, top_d=0, h, axis=Axis.Z, anchor=Anchor.CENTER) Sphere(radius, *, anchor=Anchor.CENTER) anchor selects which world-cardinal primitive datum lies at model coordinate (0, 0, 0) before later placement.
For Cylinder the anchor is resolved against its world XYZ bounds after the axis is chosen. Axis.X therefore uses LEFT/RIGHT for the axial ends; Axis.Y uses FRONT/BACK; Axis.Z uses BOTTOM/TOP. The remaining cardinal directions select tangent datums on the transverse circular bounds.
Forge lowers each primitive through the native command that SolidCraft already owns:
Box CENTER maps to native center; another Box anchor maps to the matching native corner. Cylinder always maps to native base; Forge derives that base from axis, height, diameter and the selected anchor. Cone maps to native solid.cone with diameter, top_diameter, height, axis and a derived native base. Because a cone/frustum has unequal end radii, Forge supports CENTER and the two axial end anchors only. Sphere maps to native center; Forge derives the center from the selected tangent/center anchor. The same calculation is used in direct and Boolean CSG paths. Do not add a corrective move merely to preserve an old constructor convention.
Dimension-defined sketch profiles Rectangle2D, Circle2D and RoundedRectangle2D are already centered by default from change 0018. Polygon2D and Text2D keep authored coordinates/insertion points.
Box.taper(from_z=..., inset=...) is anchor-aware: from_z is measured from the actual Box bottom face regardless of the constructor anchor.
This is intentionally a breaking cleanup while Forge remains unstable. Models that require an old base/bottom datum must state it explicitly with anchor=.
See change 0022.
data.native-sketch-pattern-and-mirror-operati:
A profile already authored in the active Sketch can seed an associative native rectangular pattern:
seed = sketch.add(Circle2D(d=20), offset=(-304, 0)) row = sketch.rectangular_pattern( seed, count=9, spacing=76, direction=Axis.X, ) sketch.mirror(row, axis=Axis.Y) The source may also be a supported Slot profile or a result returned by an earlier supported Sketch pattern/mirror operation. Pattern and mirror return Sketch operation handles; they do not expose SolidCraft curve ids.
Current limits include attached Sketch qualification, rectangular patterns, fixed 2D directions or Axis.X/Axis.Y, and mirror over the Sketch X/Y origin axes. A SolidCraft mirror keeps the entity set selected when the mirror was authored; increasing an upstream pattern count later does not automatically add the new entities to that existing mirror.
See change 0033.
data.native-slot-profiles#Native Slot profile:
Explicit Sketches support the five native SolidCraft Slot constructors:
SlotCenterToCenter2D(p0, p1, width) SlotOverall2D(p0, p1, width) SlotCenterPoint2D(center, end, width) SlotArcThreePoint2D(start, through, end, width) SlotArcCenter2D(center, start, width, *, end=None, sweep=None) All five constructors accept a positive numeric width or an editable Parameter / Expression width.
The three straight constructors also accept parameterized authored endpoints when the current Slot axis is horizontal or vertical. Forge keeps SolidCraft’s native point fields numeric, creates numeric seed geometry, and drives native length, orientation and middle-position dimensions instead. Saved-design parameter changes therefore rebuild the same native Slot history without rerunning Forge Python.
For a parameterized horizontal Slot, both authored Y coordinates must represent the same symbolic intent; the equivalent rule applies to X for a vertical Slot. Parameterized diagonal straight Slots are not supported. Fixed numeric diagonal Slots continue to use the direct native creator. Saved-design position changes may move a parameterized straight Slot on its authored side of the sketch origin; crossing an origin axis is not supported in this release.
The two arc-Slot constructors keep fixed numeric authored points in this release, while their width may be parameterized.
Slots can participate in the supported native sketch rectangular_pattern() and mirror() operations.
See change 0027.
data.occurrence-placement#Occurrence Placemen:
Placement is reserved occurrence metadata, separate from component model parameters:
left = Board( width=frame_wood_thickness, ) right = left.copy( name="right", placement=Placement( x=160, ), ) Placement(x=0, y=0, z=0, rotation=None) stores the absolute pose in the parent coordinate frame. Position values may contain Parameters or Expressions.
The component factory consumes placement= before building the reusable component definition, so placement never becomes a model parameter. There is no separate public Position object and no occurrence .at(), .move() or .rotate() for initial placement.
SolidCraft 0.42 can apply a numeric translation directly in occurrence.copy(..., translate=...). Forge uses that direct form whenever it is sufficient.
Some Placements need a second native command. Examples are a rotated copy, a symbolic position, or the first occurrence created by component.create. SolidCraft returns the real occurrence id from component.create and occurrence.copy. Forge therefore gives that returned id a named replay variable such as $board_2.
The replay document stores the variable name, not the temporary SolidCraft id. Every live run and every later replay binds the variable again from the command result before a command uses it. Forge never predicts SolidCraft browser names such as Board:2.
This keeps copy(placement=...) as one Forge operation even when SolidCraft needs more than one native command to realise the pose. The second native occurrence.move is a backend detail; it does not add a second Forge movement operation.
Placement must not create a joint.create as an implementation workaround. Attachments remain explicit relationships and Placement expressions reuse existing parameters instead of publishing helper parameters.
The replay-variable correction is recorded in change 0013.
SolidCraft 0.42 has one grounding limitation: an expression-based occurrence.move on a grounded occurrence does not follow later parameter changes. Therefore Forge leaves a physical root occurrence ungrounded when its Placement position contains Parameters or Expressions. A fixed root occurrence still uses the normal grounded behaviour. This is a backend compatibility rule, not a change to the public meaning of Placement. See change 0014.
data.on#on():
on() selects a target surface for a within-component feature.
holes = Hole(d=8, depth=Depth.THROUGH_ALL).repeat_linear( count=2, spacing=self.width - 24, axis=Axis.X, ).on(plate, face=Faces.TOP) boss = Cylinder(d=24, h=14).on(plate, face=Faces.TOP) For a Hole, face=Faces.TOP means drilling starts at the current top surface and proceeds inward. Faces is surface-selection vocabulary; it is not an assembly attachment vocabulary.
data.parameter-intent#Parameter intent:
Numeric names are part of the public API contract:
Python name Meaning Native SolidCraft parameter WIDTH = 100.0 fixed constant no _pitch = 160.0 Forge/build-time input no width = 100.0 editable model parameter yes A public model parameter that disappears before native compilation is suspicious. Forge emits ModelParameterWarning instead of silently pretending the design is still associative. Use pv() only where Python genuinely needs a concrete number.
Reusable child-component defaults are fixed unless explicitly published with component(..., include=...). For example:
Bracket = component( CornerBracket, include=("inside_corner_radius",), ) include="*" explicitly publishes all public child defaults. A mapping may publish one selected child default under a chosen shared model name.
When several parts must share one parent parameter, pass the parent Parameter or Expression directly:
bottom = BottomBoard(corner_radius=self.corner_radius) roof = RoofBoard(corner_radius=self.corner_radius) bracket = Bracket(inside_corner_radius=self.corner_radius) Forge must preserve that existing dependency instead of creating unrelated or duplicated child parameters. This contract is recorded in change 0003.
Reusable component definition identity also includes fixed build-only inputs. Forge rejects arbitrary mutable/opaque Python objects, but its own immutable selector values are valid build inputs when they reduce to deterministic primitive data. This includes public expressions such as BOTTOM + LEFT, Edges.from_profile(...), axis tokens such as X, and fixed bound offsets such as X.MIN + 10. Two different selector inputs must not share one native component definition. See change 0021.
Parameter namespacing applies only to native CAD expressions. Ordinary strings are opaque user data. A text value, material name, sketch name, feature name or font name must never be rewritten merely because one word matches a parameter name.
For example, publishing a child parameter named width may rename the native parameter reference to d1_Label_width, but Text2D("width") must still produce the literal text "width". This compiler rule is recorded in change 0015.
Parameter publication by itself is not proof that a saved design remains associative. Forge tracks dependencies carried by emitted native expressions. A public parameter with no emitted dependency triggers ModelParameterWarning. If user model code calls pv() on a parameter that also remains native elsewhere, Forge warns that only part of the model may follow later SolidCraft edits. Internal Forge numeric checks and authoring-time pick coordinates do not count as user pv() calls.
Root model classes and root @assembly classes use the same diagnostic rule. See change 0016.
data.placement-vocabulary#Placement vocabular:
Forge separates position, surface support, sketch-local placement and assembly attachment. These operations are deliberately not synonyms.
Intent Public API Meaning absolute placement shape.at(x, y, z) Place a supported shape at an absolute model coordinate. shape-relative alignment shape.at(target) Align the supported child CENTER to the target CENTER. Explicit anchor forms may extend this contract where documented. It does not select a support face. feature on a surface feature.on(target, face=Faces.TOP) Put a within-component feature on a selected target surface. explicit sketch on a body Sketch(on=target, parent=Anchor.TOP) Create a named sketch attached to the selected native SolidCraft target face. Profile coordinates are authored in that native sketch frame; Forge does not reconstruct a separate face-centre coordinate system. profile inside a sketch sketch.add(profile, anchor=None) Use the profile’s natural placement default. Dimension-defined Circle2D/Rectangle2D/RoundedRectangle2D resolve the omitted anchor to CENTER; coordinate-defined Text2D/Polygon2D keep their own coordinates. deliberate sketch-local shift sketch.add(profile, offset=(u, v)) Apply an explicit local 2D displacement. For dimension-defined profiles this shifts the centred profile; for Text2D it sets the native insertion-point displacement. occurrence position/pose Component(..., placement=Placement(...)), copy(placement=...) Declare the occurrence pose at creation/copy time in the parent coordinate frame. Placement itself does not create a joint. Forge replay variables bind the real SolidCraft occurrence ids when a later native move is needed. assembly relationship child.attach(parent, ...) Create an explicit relationship between reusable component occurrences.
data.qualification-rule#Qualification rule: A public API behaviour is not considered complete merely because one example renders correctly. It needs the appropriate Q1-Q6 evidence. A qualification fixture is evidence for this document; the fixture itself is never the API definition.
data.reference-implementations#Reference impl:
Qualification pages compare Forge with PythonSCAD, pyBOSL2 and CadQuery by default. Those references answer “how is the same modelling intent expressed elsewhere?” They are not allowed to redefine Forge behaviour.
PythonSCAD is useful as a neutral Python CSG comparison; pyBOSL2 is especially useful for anchor/attachment vocabulary; CadQuery provides a distinct object/workplane/assembly/Location comparison. If a technically meaningful reference cannot be implemented, the case must carry an explicit documented exception. A missing reference or a convenience-only exception is not qualified evidence.
data.responsibility-boundaries#Responsibility:
Python objects (SCPF) -> semantic compiler -> SolidCraft commands -> SolidCraft BRep, parameters and editable feature history Forge may perform small dimension arithmetic needed to describe design intent. It must not implement a competing CAD kernel, transform solver or mating engine.
Never silently treat numeric coordinates as robust long-lived face references. Native save/reopen and parameter-edit tests determine which relationships are truly associative.
data.signed-and-symmetric-sketch-extrusion#Si:
The current public signature is:
Sketch.extrude( distance, *, sym=False, profiles=None, exact_regions=False, ) A positive finite distance follows the sketch-plane normal. A negative finite distance reverses that normal. sym=True requires a positive finite distance and splits the extrusion equally across both sides of the sketch plane. Depth.THROUGH_ALL is available only for an attached Sketch and cannot be combined with sym=True.
Forge does not expose a second direction= argument for current Sketch extrusion. Direction is expressed by the sign of distance or by sym=True.
A standalone Sketch extrusion is a normal solid Boolean operand:
with Sketch(name="Rear recess", plane="YZ") as recess: recess.add(RoundedRectangle2D(70, 202, 20), offset=(85, 263)) cut = recess.extrude(14, sym=True) body = body - cut +, - and & lower directly to the same native solid.extrude feature with SolidCraft operations join, cut and intersect respectively. Forge does not create a temporary body/combine sequence, and the standalone Sketch remains authored on its own world/work plane.
See change 0024 and change 0043.
data.user-facing-model#User-facing model:
A model does not need @dataclass. Numeric class fields are model parameters:
class Enclosure: length = 80.0 width = 50.0 height = 30.0 wall = 2.0 A model should express relationships semantically. Do not copy coordinates from one part into another merely to make a render line up.

data: The experiment keeps the existing model routes but uses a custom CAD page type inside the shared Hextra shell.
A compact primitive model: Ø100 × 10 flange, Ø44 × 16 hub, Ø24 bore and six Ø9 bolt holes on a 70 mm PCD.
An XZ polygon extruded along Y with an edge fillet and two native SolidCraft Hole features.

One shared, hole-free CornerBracket is reused by the standalone model and the wooden HUB75 enclosure. Its native outline, inner R4 fillet and elephant-foot/outer chamfers remain editable. The older hole-containing experiment is archived separately.
A constructive solid geometry demonstration: intersect a cube with a sphere, then subtract cylinders along three axes.

A simple printable bench dog inferred from the Mini-MFT reference image: 20 mm above and 20 mm below the worktop, with a nominal Ø20 insert and a small Ø20.2 flare only at the free tip. Two perpendicular slots create four flexible legs; a larger bottom chamfer provides an insertion lead-in. There is no screw mechanism.

A second fixed cross-section of the generic GuideRail component. The aluminium shape comes from the Makita 199141-8 STEP reference and is calibrated to the TSO measured 182.50 × 10.28 mm envelope. The standalone CAD example uses 600 mm for compact visual inspection; Makita’s referenced product length is 1500 mm.

The generic GuideRail component with its default Festool profile. The aluminium cross-section comes from the FS 1400/2 STEP reference and is calibrated to the TSO measured 184.20 × 10.50 mm envelope. Only rail length is a native CAD parameter.

A separately evolvable second HUB75 display design. Its first revision deliberately matches the current five-panel wooden display geometry and parameter set, but owns its own model-local parts and assemblies so later v2 experiments do not change v1. Generic Hub75PanelBasic and CornerBracket components remain shared.

Shared panel component from the existing OpenSCAD reference: a 159.70 × 319.71 × 14.50 mm envelope with four rear pockets, six rear-side blind Ø3 mounting-hole centres and a grey housing material. Standalone uses the component’s own local XY/Z axes; screen assemblies rotate the exact same class into world XZ.

Five panels on the source project’s 800 × 320 mm nominal grid. One rear-tapered, four-bay panel component is reused at X=−320, −160, 0, 160 and 320 mm. Columns 2 and 4 reverse direction around the assembled front-to-back axis for the rear data chain, and all occurrences stand upright in XZ. R5 corners, detailed rear reinforcements, PCB and connectors remain future phases.

One clearly parametrized assembly: five lightweight HUB75 modules, 12 mm sidewalls/bottom/roof, 9 mm attached rear, 4 mm glass and four straight-mitred wooden retainers from one GlassStrip class. The roof extends 10 mm in front and 1 mm beyond the attached rear sheet. Eight printed corner brackets, two per corner, share the hole-free CornerBracket definition. The four rear brackets stop at the sidewall rear face (Y=75), before the 9 mm backboard (Y=75..84). The R4 fillets belong to the roof and bottom boards, not the glazing strips.
Reconstructs the Raspberry Pi 4 video using a rounded open-top shell, mounting bosses, connector cuts, floor vents, Pi 4 lettering and PETG material.
Rebuilds the supplied enclosure with the normal SCPF Box sketch/extrusion, followed by native Shell, Lip, Snap Fit, Boss and Rest features.
A feature-based plate: sketch, extrusion, four vertical fillets and a through-hole sketch.
Builds a centered plate with native Base, Holes and Bore sketches. One parameter-driven Ø8 hole cut is repeated by a native rectangular pattern, while a Ø24 boss is joined between the two cuts.

The first Simple MFT assembly reuses the exact worktop component and the generic GuideRail component. The rail runs along the short Y/depth direction, is centred over X=0 and rests on the parametrically shared worktop top face.

A reusable CRAFTMAKER-inspired worktop component: one 18 mm native Box, four straight 20 mm corner chamfers, 59 Ø20 dog holes on the nominal 9 × 7 / 76 mm grid with the four diagonal ring-2 positions omitted, and eight photo-measured native diagonal Slots.
Recreates the small SolidCraft Vent Plate example with a rounded 120 × 80 × 4 mm plate, one rectangular source cut and one native two-direction rectangular pattern.
